report.tagline: An app that lets cafes, bakeries and supermarkets sell their unsold food at the end of the day as cheap 'Surprise Bags', so less food gets thrown away.
report.simpleSummary: Too Good To Go is an app for rescuing food that shops would otherwise throw away. A bakery, cafe or supermarket posts a 'Surprise Bag' of leftover food, usually worth about three times what you pay. You pay in the app, for example £3.80 for a bag worth around £10, and pick it up at a set time near closing. You do not know exactly what is inside, which is part of the fun. It started in Copenhagen, Denmark, in 2015.

overview.whatItDoes: Too Good To Go runs a marketplace between food businesses with surplus food and people who want a cheap meal. Shops get some money back for food they would bin, users get food at a big discount, and less food goes to waste. It now also sells near-expiry packaged goods and is testing non-food surplus.
howItWorks: A store lists how many Surprise Bags it expects to have today, the price, and a pick-up window, often near closing time.
Users browse a map or list of nearby bags and reserve one by paying in the app.
At the pick-up time, the user shows the app at the counter and gets a bag of whatever is left that day.
Too Good To Go keeps a fixed fee per bag sold, and stores pay a yearly membership fee to list.
Users rate the bag, and stores with poor ratings get fewer bookings.
The 'Too Good To Go Parcels' and in-app shop sell boxes of near-expiry groceries delivered to the door in some countries.
overview.valueProposition: For users: good food for about a third of the price, and a small way to fight food waste. For stores: money back on food they would throw away, plus new customers walking in.

businessModel.summary: Too Good To Go earns a fixed fee on each bag sold and a yearly membership fee from each store. It holds no food and does not deliver Surprise Bags, so its costs are mostly staff, tech and marketing.

revenueStreams.detail: A fixed part of each bag's price, often around £1 in the UK.
A yearly fee each store pays to list, around £39 in the UK.
Margin on near-expiry packaged goods sold online.
Deals with big chains and brands.

businessModel.pricing: Users pay the bag price, usually £3 to £5 in the UK. Stores pay a yearly membership fee and give Too Good To Go a fixed fee per bag sold.
costDrivers: Sales teams to sign up stores
Customer support for disputes about bag contents
businessModel.unitEconomics: On a £3.80 bag, Too Good To Go might keep about £1 to £1.10, and the store keeps the rest. Card fees cost about £0.10. There is no delivery or stock cost. So most of that £1 is gross profit. The challenge is that each bag earns very little, so the company needs huge volume to pay for sales teams, support and marketing. Analysts question whether it can turn revenue growth into steady profit.

howTheyGetUsers: Viral TikTok and Instagram videos of big bags
Partnerships with big brands like Greggs, M&S and Costa
growth.moat: Too Good To Go has the largest network of food stores and users for surplus food in Europe. Stores join because users are there, and users come because stores are there. Its brand is tied to the anti-waste mission, which is hard to copy.

northStar.why: Each collected bag means food saved from the bin, a happy user and money back to a store. It captures the mission and the business together.

improvementIdeas.problem: Users get items they cannot eat.

pmLessons: A mission can drive growth and loyalty if it is easy to act on.
A surprise element can turn a constraint, unknown leftovers, into a fun feature.
Low-revenue-per-transaction models need huge scale to make money.
Two-sided marketplaces need both sides to have a good experience; one bad bag can lose a user.

interviewQuestions.question: How would you improve bag quality without losing the surprise?
interviewQuestions.hint: Separate what users hate (items they cannot eat, poor value) from what they enjoy (not knowing exactly what is coming). Suggest dietary tags and a minimum value promise, and measure average rating and 30-day repeat use.

interviewQuestions.question: How would you grow Too Good To Go in the US?
interviewQuestions.hint: Name the barriers: people drive more, chains have central waste rules, and fewer users live near each store. Pick one dense city and one partner type, like bakery chains, and set a sell-through target.

interviewQuestions.question: What is Too Good To Go's north star metric, and how would you break it down?
interviewQuestions.hint: Bags collected per week. Split it into bags listed (supply), share reserved (sell-through) and share actually collected, each with two or three inputs a team can move.

interviewQuestions.question: How would you reduce last-minute store cancellations?
interviewQuestions.hint: Find the cause first: stores overestimate leftovers or forget the bags. Suggest forecasting from past surplus and staff reminders, and track cancellation rate with store churn as a guardrail.

interviewQuestions.question: Should Too Good To Go expand beyond food?
interviewQuestions.hint: Weigh fit with the anti-waste mission, real demand and the extra complexity for stores. Suggest a small test in one market with a clear success bar before rolling out.
